title: One DocumentFragment insert vs appendChild in a loop
variable: DocumentFragment batch insert vs per-node appendChild
claim: 'Batch your inserts through a DocumentFragment' is the single most repeated piece of DOM performance advice on the web, and Gameface RAG 07-performance.md 'Throttling DOM Mutations' gives the engine-side reason: the DOM runs on the JS thread and a tight mutation loop triggers layout work. This case measures whether the fragment actually collapses that into one solve in cohtml, or whether the engine already defers layout to the end of the frame and makes the advice moot.
result: NOT CONFIRMED. NO RELIABLE DIFFERENCE at 30, 100 and 300 elements - every phase within the guardrail (largest was Layout 1.07x at 300, which fails the 1.10x size gate). The most repeated piece of DOM performance advice on the web does not reproduce as a measurable per-frame win in cohtml at up to 300 nodes rebuilt every frame. The likely reason is that the engine already defers layout to the end of the frame, so there are no repeated solves for a fragment to collapse; what the fragment saves is per-insertion bookkeeping, which is too small to clear the noise here. This is a negative result and carries the standard qualifier: no measurable difference ON THIS MACHINE, at this scale, in this cohtml version. It is not a licence to insert nodes carelessly - it says the fragment is not the lever, and the mutation volume itself is what costs.
notes: Applicability gate: DIRECT. The feature inventory flags DocumentFragment as partial with 'missing: DocumentFragment, moveBefore, prepend, replaceChildren', so it was verified manually against the Player: document.createDocumentFragment() works, appending to it works, and inserting it into the tree moves its children as expected. This case uses only createDocumentFragment/appendChild/removeChild and none of the missing members. Rule 1: one variable, how the batch reaches the live tree. Rule 2: identical DOM at the end of every frame - same nodes, same order, same positions. Rule 3: identical JS apart from the single USE_FRAGMENT constant; both pages define both insertion paths and share makeTile. Rule 4: no text, no assets. Rule 5: 300 tiles occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080. Rule 6: the rebuild IS the case and replaces the shared damage driver; it runs every frame from load in both variants, so there is no idle window. Rule 7: positions derive from the loop index only. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS. Rule 10: expected axis is Layout. NOTE: both variants pay the same teardown (the removeChild loop) and the same node construction cost; only the insertion path differs, which is what isolates the variable.
